dervis-irab:33-42.t:
* Vocabulary:
(حاصِباً): a wind that pelted them (ḥaṣabathum), i.e. pelted them with stones and pebbles (al-ḥaṣbāʾ). Al-Farazdaq said:
مستقبلين شمال الشام تضربنا ... بحاصب كنديف القطن منثور
(Facing the north wind of Syria, it strikes us with a pelting gust like scattered carded cotton.)
In al-Mukhtār: "al-ḥaṣbāʾ, with the long vowel, means pebbles; from it comes al-Muḥaṣṣab, a place in the Hijaz. Al-ḥāṣib is a violent wind that stirs up pebbles. Al-ḥaṣab, with two fatḥas, is that with which a fire is pelted (tuḥṣab), i.e. thrown into it; anything you throw into a fire, you have 'ḥaṣabta' the fire with it. Its pattern is that of ḍaraba." More on its meaning will come in the I'rab section.
(بِسَحَرٍ): saḥar, when indefinite, means one of the pre-dawn times; one says: "I saw Zayd at a pre-dawn (saḥaran), one of the pre-dawns." Had a particular day's saḥar been meant, it would have been a diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf), because it would then be definite and deflected (maʿdūl) from al-saḥar, since its proper form when definite is with al-. Al-Zamakhsharī's wording: "(بسحر): at a portion of the night, namely its last sixth. It is also said: there are two saḥars; the upper saḥar is before the breaking of dawn, and the other at its breaking. He recited:
يا سائلي إن كنت عنها تسأل ... مرّت بأعلى السحرين تذأل
(O you who ask me, if you are asking about her: she passed by at the upper of the two pre-dawns, trotting briskly.)
It is fully declined (munṣarif) because it is indefinite." Moreover, there is disagreement over the definiteness of the diptote form. It is said that it is a diptote because of definiteness and deflection ('adl). As for the definiteness, there is disagreement about it: it is said that it is definite as a proper name, because it has been made a name for this time; and it is said that it resembles a proper name, because it is definite without an overt marker, like a proper name. As for the deflection, its form is deflected from al-saḥar with al-, because when a specific one is meant, it should by origin be mentioned definite with al-; so the word with al- was abandoned while definiteness was still intended, and so it was made a diptote. Al-Suhaylī and al-Shalawbīn the Younger said it is definite [and] known, and they differed over the reason its nunation is withheld: al-Suhaylī said it is with an intended annexation (iḍāfa), and al-Shalawbīn said with an intended al-.

* I'rab:
(كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ لُوطٍ بِالنُّذُرِ): a past verb and its fāʿil (agent); (بالنذر) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (كذبت).
(إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنا عَلَيْهِمْ حاصِباً إِلَّا آلَ لُوطٍ نَجَّيْناهُمْ بِسَحَرٍ): inna and its noun, and the clause (أرسلنا) is its khabar (predicate); (عليهم) is attached to (أرسلنا); (حاصبا) is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (إلا) is a particle of exception; (آل لوط) is excepted by (إلا). In this exception there are two views. The first is that it is connected (muttaṣil), the meaning being that He sent the pelting wind upon all of them except his family, upon whom He did not send it. The second is that it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), the meaning being that He did not send it upon the family of Lot. The [correct] view is the first. (نجيناهم) is a verb and its agent, and (بسحر) is attached to (نجيناهم).
(نِعْمَةً مِنْ عِنْدِنا كَذلِكَ نَجْزِي مَنْ شَكَرَ): (نعمة) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) agreeing with its governor in meaning, namely (نجيناهم), since rescuing is a favour; or it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose) giving the reason for "anjaynāhum" — al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this and confined himself to it. [Translator's note: the source writes «أنجيناهم» here, while the verse has (نجيناهم).] (من عندنا) is a naʿt (adjective) of (نعمة). (كذلك) is attached to an omitted adjective of an omitted absolute object, i.e. "the like of that rescue". (نجزي) is an imperfect verb, nominative; (من) is a relative noun, direct object; and the clause (شكر) is the ṣila (relative clause).
(وَلَقَدْ أَنْذَرَهُمْ بَطْشَتَنا فَتَمارَوْا بِالنُّذُرِ): the wāw is a conjunction; the lām is the answer to the omitted oath; (قد) is a particle of verification; (أنذرهم) is a verb, a latent (mustatir) agent and a first direct object; (بطشتنا) is a second direct object, or it is accusative by removal of the preposition — two views. The fāʾ is a conjunction; (تماروا) is a past verb and the wāw is its agent, i.e. they pushed back the warning by way of disputation; (بالنذر) is attached to (تماروا).
(وَلَقَدْ راوَدُوهُ عَنْ ضَيْفِهِ فَطَمَسْنا أَعْيُنَهُمْ فَذُوقُوا عَذابِي وَنُذُرِ): the clause is conjoined to the preceding clause; (عن ضيفه) is attached to (راودوه); (فطمسنا) is conjoined to (راودوه); (أعينهم) is a direct object. The fāʾ is conjunctive and what it conjoins is omitted, i.e. "so We said to them"; the clause (ذوقوا) is the speech quoted by the omitted verb of saying; (عذابي) is the object of (ذوقوا); (نذر) is conjoined to (عذابي), and the yāʾ of the first person has been dropped, as preceded.
(وَلَقَدْ صَبَّحَهُمْ بُكْرَةً عَذابٌ مُسْتَقِرٌّ): also conjoined. (بكرة) is an adverb of time attached to "ṣaḥabahum" [Translator's note: so in the source, «بصحبهم»; evidently a misprint for (صبّحهم)], i.e. not on a specific day; (عذاب) is the agent, and (مستقر) is an adjective of (عذاب), i.e. it will not depart from them.
(فَذُوقُوا عَذابِي وَنُذُرِ وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِنْ مُدَّكِرٍ): its i'rab has preceded.
(وَلَقَدْ جاءَ آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ النُّذُرُ): the i'rab of its parallel has preceded.
(كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا كُلِّها فَأَخَذْناهُمْ أَخْذَ عَزِيزٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ): resumptive speech, set forth to answer a question arising from the account of the warnings' coming, as though it were said: "So what did they do then?" and it was said: "They denied." (بآياتنا) is attached to (كذبوا), and (كلها) is a tawkīd (emphasis) of (آياتنا). (فأخذناهم): the fāʾ is conjunctive, and (أخذناهم) is a verb, its agent and its direct object; (أخذ عزيز) is an absolute object, and (مقتدر) is an adjective of (عزيز); the annexation is that of the maṣdar (verbal noun) to its agent.

* Rhetoric:
Repetition (al-takrīr): in the preceding verses there is a noticeable, deliberate repetition, whose purpose is reminding and rousing from the slumber of heedlessness that may come upon minds and veil them from reflection and contemplation, and cover them with the curtains of ignorance until they can scarcely see anything. More on this device will come in Sūrat al-Raḥmān.

dervis-irab:43-55.t:
* I'rab:
(أَكُفَّارُكُمْ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أُولئِكُمْ أَمْ لَكُمْ بَراءَةٌ فِي الزُّبُرِ): (أكفاركم): the hamza is for the disapproving interrogative, which has the meaning of negation; (كفاركم) is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and (خير) is the khabar (predicate); (من أولئكم) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (خير). (أم) is the disconnected (munqaṭiʿa) one, meaning "rather" (bal); it is for turning away (iḍrāb) and moving to another aspect of rebuke. (لكم) is a fronted predicate, (براءة) is a delayed subject, and (في الزبر) is a naʿt (adjective) of (براءة).
(أَمْ يَقُولُونَ نَحْنُ جَمِيعٌ مُنْتَصِرٌ): what was said about (أم) has preceded. (يقولون) is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), and the wāw is the fāʿil (agent); (نحن) is a subject, (جميع) a predicate, and (منتصر) an adjective of (جميع), because it has the meaning of "a group" (jamʿ); the clause is the speech quoted (maqūl al-qawl). (منتصر) was made singular only on account of the form of (جميع), which is singular in form even though it is a noun for a group, like "raht" (band) and "jaysh" (army). It is also said: it did not say "muntaṣirūn" in order to agree with the verse endings — and this is good.
(سَيُهْزَمُ الْجَمْعُ وَيُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ): the sīn is a particle of the future; (يهزم) is an imperfect verb, passive; (الجمع) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (يولون) is conjoined to (سيهزم); and (الدبر) is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). It did not say "al-adbār" (backs), also to agree with the verse endings, and because it is a generic noun, since each one of them turns his back.
(بَلِ السَّاعَةُ مَوْعِدُهُمْ وَالسَّاعَةُ أَدْهى وَأَمَرُّ): (بل) is a particle of turning away and conjunction; (الساعة) is a subject and (موعدهم) its predicate; the wāw is a conjunction; (الساعة) is a subject, (أدهى) its predicate, and (أمرّ) is conjoined to (الساعة) [Translator's note: so in the source; (أمرّ) is evidently conjoined to (أدهى)]. You may also make the wāw circumstantial (for the ḥāl).
(إِنَّ الْمُجْرِمِينَ فِي ضَلالٍ وَسُعُرٍ): inna and its noun; (في ضلال) is its predicate.
(يَوْمَ يُسْحَبُونَ فِي النَّارِ عَلى وُجُوهِهِمْ ذُوقُوا مَسَّ سَقَرَ): (يوم) is an adverb (ẓarf) attached to an omitted verb of saying, i.e. "it will be said to them on the day they are dragged"; the clause (يسحبون) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation to it; (في النار) is attached to (يسحبون); (على وجوههم) is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial); (ذوقوا) is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the nūn, and the wāw is its agent; the clause is the speech quoted by the implied verb of saying. (مسّ) is a direct object and (سقر) a muḍāf ilayhi (the second term of the genitive construct); it is a proper name for Hell, and that is why it is a diptote, since it is a feminine proper name.
(إِنَّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْناهُ بِقَدَرٍ): inna and its noun. (كل شيء) is accusative by way of ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb), by an omitted verb explained by what follows it, i.e. "We created everything; We created it"; the clause of the omitted verb is in the position of the nominative as the predicate of (إنّا), and the clause (خلقناه) is explicative, with no grammatical position. A long dispute has arisen over this verse, which we have summarised for you in the Benefits section. (بقدر) is attached to an omitted ḥāl of (كل), i.e. measured out, perfected and ordered.
(وَما أَمْرُنا إِلَّا واحِدَةٌ كَلَمْحٍ بِالْبَصَرِ): the wāw is conjunctive; (ما) is negating; (أمرنا) is a subject; (إلا) is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); (واحدة) is the predicate of (أمرنا); (كلمح) is attached to an omitted ḥāl of the object of the command, namely the thing commanded into existence, i.e. in the state of its coming into being swiftly; (بالبصر) is attached to (لمح).
(وَلَقَدْ أَهْلَكْنا أَشْياعَكُمْ فَهَلْ مِنْ مُدَّكِرٍ): the i'rab of its parallel has preceded shortly before.
(وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ فِي الزُّبُرِ): the wāw is conjunctive; (كل) is a subject and (شيء) a muḍāf ilayhi; the clause (فعلوه) is an adjective; (في الزبر) is the predicate, i.e. the books, plural of "zabūr".
(وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍ وَكَبِيرٍ مُسْتَطَرٌ): a subject and predicate, i.e. written down in the Preserved Tablet.
(إِنَّ الْمُتَّقِينَ فِي جَنَّاتٍ وَنَهَرٍ): inna and its noun; (في جنات) is its predicate; (نهر) is conjoined to (جنات).
(فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ): the preposition and its genitive noun are a badal (substitute) of part for whole from His words (في جنات), because the seat is part of the gardens; or you may attach it to an omitted [word] as a second predicate of (إنّ). (عند مليك) is an adverb attached to an omitted adjective of (جنات) or of (مقعد); it is also said to be a second or third predicate of (إنّ). (مليك) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha).

* Benefits:
1- A dispute arose between Ahl al-Sunna and the Muʿtazila over the words of Allah the Exalted (إنّا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر). The rule laid down by the grammarians would call for the nominative of (كل), yet none of the Seven read it so, because with the nominative the speech is a single clause and with the accusative it is two clauses, so the nominative is more concise; moreover, there is nothing here requiring the accusative from any of the six categories, namely command, prohibition, interrogative, wish, hope and urging. Nor do we find here a fitting conjunction or anything else of the places they count as making the accusative preferable. Once this is clear, it is known that the nominative was abandoned by consensus only for a subtle secret that determines the choice of the accusative: had it been nominative, the clause (خلقناه) would fall as an adjective of (شيء), and (بقدر) would be raised as the predicate of "everything" restricted by the adjective, and the speech would amount to: "Indeed, everything created by Us is by measure." That would suggest that some created thing attributed to other than Allah the Exalted is not by measure. With the accusative, the speech becomes: "Indeed, We created everything by measure," which conveys the universality of the attribution of every created thing to Allah the Exalted. Since this benefit is not matched by the verbal benefit [of concision] in the nominative reading, together with the deficiency of meaning in the nominative, and with the meaning coming complete like the break of dawn in this widely transmitted reading, it is no wonder they agreed unanimously to abandon the nominative for the accusative.
However, al-Zamakhsharī — one of the heads and leading figures of the Muʿtazila — tried to breach the consensus and reported a reading in the nominative, with (خلقناه) in the position of the adjective and (بقدر) as the predicate, or the clause (خلقناه) as the predicate and (بقدر) a ḥāl. His wording is: "(كل شيء) is accusative by an implied (muḍmar) verb explained by the overt one; and it was read (كل شيء) in the nominative." Abū al-Sammāl alone read it so, and it is anomalous (shādhdha).
2- A thorough summary of the topic of ishtighāl (preoccupation): here is a thorough summary of the topic of ishtighāl.
As for its definition: it is that a noun comes first and there comes after it a fully conjugable verb, or a noun resembling one, that puts in the accusative a pronoun referring to it, or something connected with its pronoun, either through an intermediary or otherwise; and that governor is such that, were it freed from that governed word and given power over the preceding noun, it would put it in the accusative. The accusative is obligatory when the preceding noun comes after something specific to verbs, such as the particles of urging, e.g. "hallā Zaydan akramtahu" (why not honour Zayd?); the interrogative particles other than the hamza, e.g. "hal Zaydan raʾaytahu" (did you see Zayd?); and the conditional particles, e.g. "ḥaythumā Zaydan laqītahu fa-akrimhu" (wherever you meet Zayd, honour him). The accusative is preferable in six cases:
1- That the preoccupied verb is a request, namely a command or a supplication for good or ill.
2- That the preoccupied verb is joined to the lām or the lā of request, e.g. "ʿAmran li-yaḍribhu Bakr" (ʿAmr — let Bakr strike him) and "Khālidan lā tuhinhu" (Khālid — do not insult him).
3- That the noun from which [the verb] is preoccupied comes after something that is mostly followed by a verb. There are examples of this, among them the interrogative hamza, e.g. (أبشرا منّا واحدا نتبعه).
4- That the noun from which [the verb] is preoccupied comes after a conjunction not separated by "ammā" (with fatḥa on the hamza and doubled mīm), preceded by a verb not built on a noun before it, e.g. "qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmran akramtuhu" (Zayd stood, and ʿAmr I honoured), and the words of the Exalted (والأنعام خلقها لكم); as opposed to e.g. "ḍarabtu Zaydan wa-ammā ʿAmrun fa-ahantuhu" (I struck Zayd, and as for ʿAmr, I insulted him), where the preferred is the nominative.
5- That with the nominative it might be imagined that the verb preoccupied with the pronoun is an adjective of what precedes it, e.g. (إنّا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر). For if (كل) were nominative, (خلقناه) could be its predicate, and the meaning would be the universality of the creation of existing beings by measure, whether good or evil, as is the doctrine of the Sunna; and (خلقناه) could be an adjective of (شيء) with (بقدر) the predicate of (كل). Specification by the adjective suggests that what is not described by it is not by measure; the adjective is the createdness attributed to Him, so createdness not attributed to Him would not be by measure, which suggests that there is something created by other than Him, the Exalted — and that is the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. That is not imagined with the accusative of (كل), as the object of an omitted verb explained by (خلقنا); and it is impossible to make it an adjective of (كل شيء), because the adjective does not govern the qualified noun, and what does not govern does not explain a governor. Hence the nominative of (كل) is obligatory if the verb attached to the pronoun is an adjective of (كل شيء), e.g. (وكل شيء فعلوه في الزبر), i.e. the books. The accusative of (كل) is not valid here, because supposing the verb to be given power over it is only according to the intended meaning, and the meaning here is not that they did everything in the books, such that (فعلوا) could be given power over (كل شيء); rather the meaning is: everything done by them is recorded in the books, which differs from that meaning. So the nominative of (كل) is obligatory as a subject; the later verb is an adjective of it or of (شيء), and (في الزبر) is the predicate of (كل).
Moreover, Sībawayh did not consider the suggestion of an adjective a reason for preferring the accusative, as Ibn Mālik did; rather Sībawayh made the accusative the less preferred option in the verse mentioned. He said: "As for the words of the Exalted (إنّا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر), it came only after the manner of 'Zaydan ḍarabtuhu' (Zayd — I struck him), and that is good, abundant Arabic." Ibn al-Shajarī said: "The Basrans agreed regarding this verse that the nominative is preferable, since nothing precedes that requires the accusative; the Kufans said: the accusative is better in it, because a governor that puts in the accusative precedes (كل), namely (إنّ), and that called for implying (خلقنا)."
6- The sixth case in which the accusative is preferable: that the noun from which [the verb] is preoccupied is an answer to a question [whose interrogative word is] put in the accusative by what follows it, like "Zaydan ḍarabtuhu" (Zayd I struck) in answer to one who said: "Which of them did you strike?" or "Whom did you strike?" — Zayd is preferably accusative because it is an answer to the question, so that the answer matches the question as a verbal clause.
Moreover, in His words (وكل شيء فعلوه في الزبر), the nominative of (كل) is obligatory and its accusative impossible, because supposing the verb to be given power over it is only according to the intended meaning, and the meaning here is not that they did everything in the books, such that (فعلوا) could be given power over (كل شيء); the later verb is an adjective of it or of (شيء).
